title.en: Number play: parity, divisibility tests and digits in disguise

text.en: Anshu wonders: can every natural number be written as a sum of consecutive numbers? Which numbers can be written in more than one way? Can zero be written like that?

Sums of consecutive numbers show patterns: 2 + 3 = 5 and 3 + 4 + 5 = 12, and every odd number is the sum of two consecutive numbers.
Parity tells whether a number is odd or even, and parity rules say even + even = even, odd + odd = even, and odd + even = odd.
If we put plus and minus signs between four numbers in all 8 ways, every result has the same parity, because changing a plus to a minus changes the value by an even number.
A number is a multiple of 2 if its units digit is even, a multiple of 5 if it ends in 0 or 5, and a multiple of 10 if it ends in 0.
A number is divisible by 3 (or 9) if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3 (or 9).
A number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits form a multiple of 4, and by 8 if its last three digits form a multiple of 8.
For 11, add the digits at odd places and the digits at even places; the number is divisible by 11 if the difference is 0 or a multiple of 11.
We can explain each test with algebra: for example 100a + 10b + c leaves the same remainder as a + b + c when divided by 9 or 3.
Digits in disguise are puzzles where letters stand for digits, like AB + AB = BAB, and we solve them by logic about carries and parity.
Always test a guess in the whole puzzle, because a solution must satisfy every column.

prompt.en: Explain why the digit-sum test for 3 works.

requiredIdeas.en: Powers of 10 leave remainder 1 on division by 3.
So 100a + 10b + c has the same remainder as a + b + c.
Hence the number is divisible by 3 exactly when the digit sum is.

commonMisconceptions.en: A number ending in 3 is divisible by 3.

points.en: Parity rules: even + even = even, odd + odd = even, odd + even = odd.
Divisibility tests for 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10 and 11 use digits.
Algebra explains why the tests work and puzzles use the same logic.
